issues.legal_issue: A wife is not a judicially separated wife for purposes of exclusion from a tenure-holder’s family holding when the separation rests on a settlement recorded by a body lacking authority to decide matrimonial disputes, rather than an order of a competent court.
material_facts: A wife had brought criminal proceedings concerning her husband's second marriage, and while those proceedings were pending the spouses entered a settlement recorded by a local panchayat.
The settlement provided that the spouses would live separately, that the wife would receive land for maintenance, and that their marital relationship would be treated as ended.
The land transferred under the settlement was included in the husband's holding in ceiling proceedings.
No competent court had made an order for judicial separation.
issues.conclusion: The wife was not a judicially separated wife under Section 3(7) of the Ceiling Act. The land was therefore not excluded from the husband's holding on that ground, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(7) of the U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960 excludes a judicially separated spouse from the definition of family. 'Judicially' requires separation ordered or recognised through a judicial proceeding before a competent court; separate living by agreement or through a panchayat is insufficient. Sections 10 and 19 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, and Section 23 of the Indian Divorce Act, 1869, illustrate court-ordered judicial separation. The Court approved the approach in Sarju Prasad v. 4th Additional District Judge (1980 All LJ 515) and rejected the contrary interpretation in Gangotri Devi v. State (1982 All LJ 103).

rule.if: ceiling_holding_case and separate_living_fixed_by_compromise and settlement_recorded_by_body_without_matrimonial_authority and not competent_court_separation_order

predicates.ceiling_holding_case: The dispute concerns whether a spouse or property is included in a tenure-holder's ceiling holding.
predicates.separate_living_fixed_by_compromise: The spouses' separate living was arranged through an agreement or compromise.
predicates.settlement_recorded_by_body_without_matr: A body without authority to decide matrimonial disputes recorded the arrangement concerning the spouses' separation.
predicates.competent_court_separation_order: A competent court made an order for judicial separation.

issues.definition: When a ceiling-holding dispute involves separate living arranged by compromise and recorded by a body without matrimonial authority, with no competent-court separation order, the wife is not treated as judicially separated.

issues.legal_issue: A power to record or decide disputes according to a written compromise does not give a local adjudicatory body authority to decide a dispute outside its otherwise conferred subject-matter jurisdiction.
material_facts: The panchayat recorded a written compromise addressing the spouses' marital status and separation.
The governing law conferred limited civil jurisdiction on the panchayat, including certain claims concerning money and movable property, but did not confer jurisdiction over matrimonial matters.
The parties relied on the statutory provision allowing the panchayat to decide a dispute according to a written settlement or compromise.
issues.conclusion: The consent provision did not confer extraordinary or special jurisdiction on the panchayat. It permitted an order by consent only in a dispute otherwise cognizable and within the panchayat's jurisdiction, so it could not authorize the matrimonial determination in the compromise.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 64 and 82 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, must be read together: Section 82 enables disposition by consent of disputes that the panchayat is otherwise empowered to decide, but does not enlarge its subject-matter jurisdiction. A written compromise cannot confer jurisdiction over a dispute outside that authority.

predicates.consent_jurisdiction_case: The issue concerns whether an adjudicatory body's power to act on consent extends to a particular dispute.
predicates.dispute_outside_body_conferred_subject_m: The dispute concerns a subject that the body is not otherwise authorized to decide.
predicates.parties_agreed_in_writing: The parties agreed in writing that the body should decide the dispute according to their settlement or compromise.

issues.definition: When parties agree in writing to submit a dispute outside an adjudicatory body's authorized subject matter, their agreement does not give the body jurisdiction to decide it.
